newsitem.title: GERMANY: INTERVIEW-German funds heading for trillion marks.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-German funds heading for trillion marks.

text.p: Changes in saving patterns could lead to the total of funds under management in Germany hitting a trillion marks by the year 2000, Rolf Passow, head of the German investment funds association, BVI, said on Tuesday.

"The current level of 700 billion marks ($463.5 billion) invested in retail funds and specialised funds, including Luxembourg, which took 40 years to build up, could reach one trillion marks by the year 2000," said Passow.

Passow was elected management board chairman of the BVI last month and was speaking in an interview with Reuters. Passow is the managing director of Dresdner Bank's asset management arm, Deutsche Investment Trust.

"In the last few years we have seen more new developments in the investment funds sector than in the previous ten or fifteen years and are profiting from growth in financial assets in this country to the tune of 260 billion marks per year."
"We are also seeing what is basically healthy economic development here," said Passow.

The main driver behind the fund management industry will be the growth in private pension provision as governments struggle to pay state pensions as the population grows older, Passow said, a problem also facing other European countries.
Once German investors realise the limitations of the state pension scheme, there will be a change in approach in how people view investment funds.
"The pension fund business is a good foundation for the capital markets generally," said Passow,

German investors are traditionally conservative and value security above almost all else when it comes to investment. Are Germans ready to throw away their savings books and safer bonds and make the leap into slightly-riskier investment vehicles?
"The generation after the second world war learned that the investment security was of absolute importance and this way of thinking is still very important," said Passow.
"There is a change in the way people think, however, and this will boost the fund management industry," he added.
"The move from state pension provision to private provision will not happen in this century, but you will be able to see a change in trend over the the next few months," said Passow.
That a change is taking place is evident from BVI's recent quarterly report, which showed a total of 1.7 billion marks invested in international equity funds in the first nine months of this year.

Conservatism is also part of the German investment scene. For example, when derivative instruments were first introduced into Germany, the law had to be changed so they did not come under the country's archaic gaming laws.

Passow says that imminent legislation for the financial services industry will make the market easier to operate in, and products such as non-bourse risk management products and pyramid funds could soon be introduced.
As far as competition from foreign fund management companies goes, Passow seems unworried. "I don't know of any foreign fund management companies which are offering cheaper funds," he said.
Many foreign funds include entry and exit costs and administration charges which are higher than those charged by their German equivalents.
He says that administration charges are very necessary.
"Most investors need investment advice, and investment advice costs money," he said.
With European currency union now just around the corner, Passow is confident that German fund management companies will be able to fight their corner in a single European market.
"There will still be regional centres when EMU arrives, and for German fund management companies, the centre will still be Germany," said Passow.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.510 German Marks)
